```{r}
#| label: setup
library(card)
```

MAUDE is the FDA's database of medical device adverse event reports, filed by manufacturers, importers and device user facilities under a mandatory reporting requirement, and by clinicians, patients and consumers voluntarily.
It is a passive surveillance system, so a count of reports is a count of filings rather than of events, and the denominator of devices in use is never given.

{card} covers four steps against it: querying openFDA for reports, filling in the narratives openFDA withholds, mapping the free-text manufacturer and brand strings onto entities, and grouping the coded problem terms into clinical complications.
Chunks that reach FDA are not evaluated when this vignette is built, while everything shown against bundled data is.

# Querying

`maude_query()` builds the search string, paginates, and returns one row per report.

```{r}
#| eval: false
events <- maude_query(
  device_generic_name = "catheter, percutaneous",
  date_start = as.Date("2024-01-01"),
  date_end = as.Date("2024-12-31"),
  limit = 500
)
```

`limit` caps the whole call rather than each request.
A query matching more reports than `limit` returns is truncated with a warning, and the number that actually matched is carried on the result:

```{r}
#| eval: false
attr(events, "total")
```

## Search syntax

openFDA reads *Elasticsearch* query syntax, and `search` takes it verbatim.
The field arguments and `...` are conveniences that build the same string, so anything they cannot express can be written out by hand.

| What you want | How it is written |
|---|---|
| A bare term anywhere in the record | `"pacemaker"` |
| One field | `"device.generic_name:pacemaker"` |
| Two conditions | `"device.generic_name:pacemaker AND event_type:malfunction"` |
| Either of two values | `"device.brand_name:(farawave OR farapulse)"` |
| A phrase, rather than its words | `"device.brand_name:\"arctic front\""` |
| A date range | `"date_received:[20200101 TO 20201231]"` |
| Records where a field is missing | `"_missing_:date_of_event"` |

The field names are openFDA's own and are listed at <https://open.fda.gov/apis/device/event/searchable-fields/>.
They change from time to time, so that list is the authority rather than this page.

These three calls send the same query:

```{r}
#| eval: false
maude_query(search = "device.brand_name:farawave AND event_type:malfunction")

maude_query(device_brand_name = "FARAWAVE", event_type = "Malfunction")

maude_fda_api_call(
  search_query = "device.brand_name:farawave AND event_type:malfunction",
  limit = 100
)
```

`maude_query()` is the one to reach for.
`maude_fda_api_call()` sends a single request as written, which is what you want for custom pagination, for the count endpoint below, or for a query the argument list cannot express.

## Counting without retrieving

A frequency table does not need the records.
The openFDA count endpoint aggregates on the server and returns one term and its count per distinct value, which turns hundreds of paginated requests into one:

```{r}
#| eval: false
problems <- maude_fda_api_call(
  search_query = "device.device_report_product_code:QZI",
  count = "product_problems.exact",
  limit = 999
)
```

The `.exact` suffix counts whole field values.
Without it openFDA counts individual tokens, so `"Cardiac Tamponade"` is split into `"cardiac"` and `"tamponade"`.

Two things to hold onto.
The endpoint returns at most 1000 terms and offers no way to page past them, so check whether the result has hit that cap before treating it as complete.
And the counts are of mentions rather than of reports, since a report coded with three problems contributes to three terms.

## Narratives

openFDA returns the narrative for many reports and not for others.
`descriptions_from_web = TRUE` fills the gaps, first from FDA's bulk narrative archives, which are downloaded once and cached, and then from the MAUDE detail page of each report still missing one.

```{r}
#| eval: false
events <- maude_query("pacemaker", limit = 100, descriptions_from_web = TRUE)
```

The second pass costs one request per report, which is why it is off by default.

# Coding tables

FDA codes each report against annexed term lists, and the annexes are bundled:

```{r}
#| label: annex
annex_a <- maude_codes("A")
head(annex_a[, c("imdrf_code", "term", "level_1")], 4)
```

FDA codes a substantial share of reports at the family level, so `"Material Integrity Problem"` is a value that appears in the data and not merely a heading above it.
Joining returned terms on `term` therefore picks up leaf and family codings alike, and `level_1` rolls either up to its family.

# Manufacturers, brands and owners

`manufacturer_name` is the manufacturing entity as the reporter typed it, which is the plant rather than the company.
Counting the raw strings splits one maker across its plants and hides another behind its contract manufacturer:

```{r}
#| label: manufacturer
maude_normalize_manufacturer(c(
  "BIOSENSE WEBSTER, INC. (JUAREZ)",
  "FARAPULSE, INC.",
  "VENUSA DE MEXICO S.A. DE C.V.",
  "SOME COMPANY NOT IN THE REGISTRY"
))
```

A string the registry does not cover returns `NA` rather than a guess.

Normalising happens after the reports are in hand, which is no help for the reports a query never asked for.
A filter on `"Abbott"` reaches nothing St. Jude Medical filed before 2017, and a result missing twenty years of reports looks exactly like one that is not.
`maude_search_terms()` runs the other way, from a company to every name its reports have been filed under:

```{r}
#| label: search-terms
maude_search_terms("Abbott")
```

Pass those terms to the query, and the family comes back whole:

```{r}
#| eval: false
abbott <- maude_search_terms("Abbott")
maude_query(manufacturer_name = abbott$term, limit = 1000)
```

`from` and `to` are the window during which the company owned that entity, so `as_of` narrows the set to a point in time.
Abbott's set in 2016 is Abbott alone.
`maude_query()` warns when a manufacturer filter names a company whose other names were left out, so the omission is said out loud rather than discovered later.

Ablation modality comes from the brand, since the product code does not determine it -- `OAE` covers cryoablation and radiofrequency alike:

```{r}
#| label: ablation
maude_normalize_ablation(c(
  "FARAWAVE PULSED FIELD ABLATION CATHETER",
  "ARCTIC FRONT ADVANCE PRO",
  "PENTARAY NAV"
))
```

`PENTARAY NAV` is matched but has no modality, because a mapping catheter delivers no energy.
That is different from an unmatched brand, and `platform` tells the two apart.

Who owns an entity changes with time, which is why it is resolved separately and why `as_of` has no default:

```{r}
#| label: ownership
maude_resolve_owner("Farapulse", as_of = as.Date(c("2019-01-01", "2024-01-01")))
```

Pass `Sys.Date()` for the company that owns the entity now, or a report's `date_received` for the company that owned it when the report was filed.
The two answer different questions, and picking one silently would answer the question you did not ask.

Ownership is dated rather than a company name written next to each entity, which is what lets one acquisition be one row and lets an entity change hands twice.
Cordis was Johnson & Johnson's, then Cardinal Health's from 2015, then Hellman & Friedman's from 2021:

```{r}
#| label: cordis
maude_resolve_owner(
  rep("Cordis", 3),
  as_of = as.Date(c("2010-01-01", "2018-01-01", "2024-01-01"))
)
```

The facts behind all of this are in `maude_entities()`, one row per entity per ownership interval, each dated row citing the announcement it came from.

# Complications

The coded problem terms are FDA's vocabulary rather than a clinical one, so they are grouped into complication families before analysis:

```{r}
#| label: complications
maude_term_to_complication(c(
  "Cardiac Tamponade",
  "Low blood pressure / hypotension",
  "Unknown (for use when the device problem is not known)"
))
```

A term can land in more than one family, and anything unmatched is returned under `not_indexed`.

The terms say a complication is plausible, and the narrative says whether it happened.
`maude_adjudicate()` sends each candidate family, and only the candidates, to an **{ellmer}** chat with a schema of one boolean per classification:

```{r}
#| eval: false
chat <- ellmer::chat_openai(model = "gpt-4.1-mini")

maude_adjudicate(
  terms = "Pericardial Effusion; Low blood pressure / hypotension",
  event_narrative = events$event_description[[1]],
  chat_object = chat
)
```

The result carries the model, a hash of the system prompt, and a hash of the definitions used.
Both the prompt and the definitions change over time, and a dataset adjudicated under one pair is not comparable to a dataset adjudicated under another, so keep those attributes beside the flags.
